```{r setup, include = FALSE}

  collapse = TRUE,

  fig.align = "center",
  fig.height = 4,
  fig.width = 4

**Abstract.** EcoPhyloSim simulates the joint ecological and evolutionary dynamics
of a species community in space. Individuals on a grid die and are replaced by
offspring that disperse locally or globally, inherit and evolve traits, and are
selected by the environment and by competition with their neighbors, while new
species arise by speciation. The simulation records the spatial distribution of
the species, their traits and their phylogeny, and the package provides
functions to plot and summarize these outputs, such as species–area curves,
rank–abundance curves and measures of phylogenetic structure. This vignette
describes the model, shows how to run it and analyze its output, and documents
how the main patterns produced by the model respond to its parameters, compared
with expectations from theory and earlier studies.

# Quick start

A simulation on a grid of 50 × 50 cells with local dispersal, run for 1,000
generations:

```{r quickstart, results = 'hide', fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5, fig.cap = "Phylogeny, mean traits and spatial distribution of the species at the end of the quick-start simulation."}
library(EcoPhyloSim)
pars <- createCompletePar(x = 50, y = 50, dispersal = 1, runs = 1000,
                          specRate = 2, seed = 1)
simu <- runSimulation(pars)
plot(simu)
```

`createCompletePar()` collects the parameters of the model, `runSimulation()`
runs it, and `plot()` shows the phylogeny of the species, their mean traits and
their spatial distribution; the following chapters explain each step.

## Citation

To cite the package, use the citation information provided with the package:

```{r citation}
citation("EcoPhyloSim")
```

# Model description

The model is an individual-based, spatially explicit simulation of a species
community. The figure gives an overview of one generation; the sections below
describe the state variables, the ecological processes and the speciation
mechanisms. The symbols refer to the arguments of `createCompletePar()`; the
tables give their default values and the ranges that `createCompletePar()` and
`runSimulation()` check (see also `?createCompletePar`).

```{r schema, echo = FALSE, fig.width = 6.5, fig.height = 4.2, fig.cap = "One generation of the model. Deaths and replacements are repeated until x · y individuals have died; then new species arise, and the state is recorded at the generations given in runs."}
op <- par(mar = c(0, 0, 0, 0))
plot(NULL, xlim = c(-0.5, 10), ylim = c(0.3, 7), axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "")
box3 <- function(x, y, label, w = 4.2, h = 0.75, col = "#e8f0f7") {
  rect(x - w / 2, y - h / 2, x + w / 2, y + h / 2, col = col, border = "#0072B2")
  text(x, y, label, cex = 0.75)
}
ys <- c(6.3, 5.1, 3.9, 2.7, 1.5)
box3(2.6, ys[1], "Draw a random cell")
box3(2.6, ys[2], "Does the individual die?\nfitness < U(0, 1), or every k-th draw")
box3(2.6, ys[3], "Choose a parent\nglobal or dispersal kernel")
box3(2.6, ys[4], "Offspring inherits species and traits;\ntraits evolve")
box3(2.6, ys[5], "Update the competition term\nof the neighbors")
box3(7.6, 3.9, "Speciation:\nPoisson(specRate) new species", col = "#fbeee6")
box3(7.6, 2.7, "Record the state\n(generations in runs)", col = "#fbeee6")
arrows(2.6, ys[-5] - 0.38, 2.6, ys[-1] + 0.38, length = 0.07)
# survives: draw the next cell
segments(0.5, ys[2], 0.2, ys[2]); segments(0.2, ys[2], 0.2, ys[1])
arrows(0.2, ys[1], 0.5, ys[1], length = 0.07)
text(0.2, mean(ys[1:2]), "survives", srt = 90, cex = 0.65, pos = 2, offset = 0.3)
# repeat until x * y individuals have died, then speciation
segments(4.7, ys[5], 5.1, ys[5]); segments(5.1, ys[5], 5.1, ys[1])
arrows(5.1, ys[1], 4.7, ys[1], length = 0.07)
text(5.15, 5.4, "repeat until\nx · y deaths", cex = 0.65, pos = 4)
arrows(5.1, 3.9, 5.5, 3.9, length = 0.07)
arrows(7.6, 3.52, 7.6, 3.08, length = 0.07)
# next generation
segments(7.6, 2.32, 7.6, 0.6); segments(7.6, 0.6, 9.85, 0.6); segments(9.85, 0.6, 9.85, 6.85)
segments(9.85, 6.85, 2.6, 6.85); arrows(2.6, 6.85, 2.6, 6.68, length = 0.07)
text(9.85, 3.6, "next generation", srt = 90, cex = 0.65, pos = 2, offset = 0.15)
par(op)
```

## State variables

**The grid:** the simulation runs on a spatially discrete grid. Each cell is
occupied by one individual at any time. Each cell has an environmental value
(see Environment below). To avoid boundary effects, the boundaries of the grid
are wrapped (torus).

**Individuals:** each individual has three traits in $[0, 1]$: an
environmental trait, a competition trait and a neutral trait. Their dynamics
are described in the section on ecological processes.

**Species and phylogeny:** each individual belongs to a species. Species
properties are described by the mean of the respective traits of all
individuals of the species. The species traits serve as an attractor in the
individual trait evolution process. Further, each species contains information
about its parent species and the species that emerged from it, which gives rise
to the overall phylogeny.

**Initial state:** at the start, all individuals belong to one species and all
their traits are 0.5.

| Argument | Meaning | Default | Range |
|---|---|---|---|
| `x`, `y` | grid dimensions (cells) | 50, 50 | integers $\ge 1$, $x \cdot y \ge 2$ |
| `airmat` | environment of the cells (see Environment below) | 1 (default gradient) | single value or matrix with $y$ rows and $x$ columns, values in $[0, 1]$ |

## Ecological processes

The simulation runs over a defined number of generations. In each generation,
individuals die and are replaced by offspring with slightly changed traits
(steps 1--3 below), until $x \cdot y$ individuals have died; then new species
arise (next section), and the state of the community is recorded if the
generation is one of those given in `runs`.

**1. Mortality and replacement.** Cells are drawn at random (with replacement)
until $J = x \cdot y$ individuals have died, so some individuals die several
times per generation and others not at all. If fitness acts on mortality
(`environment`, `density`, `redQueen` or `redQueenStrength` > 0, and
`fitnessActsOn` is `"mortality"` or `"both"`), a drawn individual $i$ dies
only if its fitness $w_i$ (step 3 below) is smaller than a uniform random
number $u \sim U(0, 1)$; otherwise it survives and the next cell is drawn.
Every $k$-th draw, with $k$ = `fitnessBaseMortalityRatio`, kills the drawn
individual regardless of its fitness. $k$ therefore controls the strength of
selection: with $k = 1$ all deaths are random, and the model is neutral if
fitness acts only on mortality, even if `environment` or `density` are > 0. If
fitness does not act on mortality, every draw kills.

The dead individual is replaced by the offspring of a parent. With global
dispersal, the parent is drawn uniformly from all other cells; the dead
individual is never its own parent. With local dispersal, it is drawn from the
cells within the radius $R$ (excluding the cell itself), with weights

$$ K(d) = \exp\left(-\frac{d}{\delta}\right), $$

where $d$ is the Euclidean distance, $R = \lfloor 2 \cdot \texttt{dispersal}
\rfloor$ and $\delta = R / 2$; only multiples of 0.5 of `dispersal` therefore
have an effect. The neighborhood is a discretized circle: all cells with
$|\Delta x| \le R$ and $|\Delta y| \le \lfloor\sqrt{R^2 - \Delta x^2}\rfloor$.
If fitness acts on reproduction (`fitnessActsOn = "reproduction"` or
`"both"`, possible only with local dispersal unless the model is neutral), the
weights of the potential parents are multiplied by their fitness, if
`environment` or `density` is > 0.

| Argument | Meaning | Default | Range |
|---|---|---|---|
| `fitnessBaseMortalityRatio` | every $k$-th draw kills regardless of fitness | 10 | integer $\ge 1$; 1 gives a neutral model if fitness acts only on mortality |
| `fitnessActsOn` | whether fitness acts on mortality, reproduction or both | `"mortality"` | `"mortality"`, `"reproduction"`, `"both"`; with global dispersal only if `environment`, `density`, `redQueen` and `redQueenStrength` are 0 |
| `dispersal` | `"global"` (or 0), or the dispersal distance | `"global"` | `"global"`, 0 or $\ge 0.5$ with $2R + 1 \le \min(x, y)$; only multiples of 0.5 have an effect |

**2. Trait evolution.** The offspring inherits the species and the three traits
(environmental, competition and neutral trait) of its parent. Each trait then
changes by a small random step and is attracted towards the mean trait of its
species:

$$ t' = (1 - \alpha)\cdot t_{\mathrm{p}} + \alpha \cdot \bar t + r, $$

where $t'$ is the offspring's trait value, $t_{\mathrm{p}}$ the parent's,
$\bar t$ is the mean trait value of the species, $\alpha = 0.2$ is a fixed
attraction weight, and $r$ is drawn uniformly from $[-0.01, 0.01]$. Values outside $[0, 1]$ are reflected at the boundary.

**3. Fitness.** The fitness of individual $i$ is the sum of an environmental
and a competition term, each included only if the corresponding parameter is
> 0:

$$ w_i = \underbrace{e \cdot \exp\left(-\frac{(E_i - t_i)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right) + 1 - e}_{\text{if } e > 0} \; + \; \underbrace{c \cdot D_i + 1 - c}_{\text{if } c > 0}, $$

where $e$ = `environment`, $E_i$ is the environment of the cell, $t_i$ is the
environmental trait of the individual, $\sigma$ = `nicheWidth` is the width of
the niche, and $c$ = `density`. $D_i$ is the mean absolute difference between
the competition trait $a_i$ of the individual and those of its neighbors within
the radius $R_D$ = `densityCut` (same discretized circle as for dispersal),

$$ D_i = \frac{\sum_{j \ne i} |a_i - a_j|}{n}, $$

where $n$ is the number of cells in the neighborhood, including the focal cell.
$D_i$ is updated whenever an individual in the neighborhood is replaced.

Some consequences of this formula:

- Each term is at least $1 - e$ or $1 - c$. If both terms are included, $w_i$
  can exceed 1; such individuals survive every draw except the
  fitness-independent ones (every $k$-th draw).
- All individuals start with the same traits (0.5), so $D_i = 0$ at the start
  and density dependence acts only after the competition traits have diverged.

| Argument | Meaning | Default | Range |
|---|---|---|---|
| `environment` | weight $e$ of the environmental fitness term | 0 | $[0, 1]$ |
| `nicheWidth` | width $\sigma$ (standard deviation) of the environmental niche | 0.0366 | $> 0$; a message outside $[0.003, 3]$ (if `environment` > 0) |
| `density` | weight $c$ of the competition fitness term | 0 | $[0, 1]$ |
| `densityCut` | radius $R_D$ of the competition neighborhood | 1 | integer $\ge 1$, $\le \min(x, y)$; $2R_D + 1 \le \min(x, y)$ if `density` > 0 |

**Environment.** If no `airmat` is given, the environment varies only along the
x-axis: it is $1 - |2i/x - 1|$ in column $i = 0, \dots, x - 1$, i.e., it
increases linearly in steps of $2/x$ from 0 in the first column to its maximum in
the middle and then decreases again. The maximum is 1 for even $x$ and $(x-1)/x$
for odd $x$; for even $x$ all values except the minimum and maximum occur in two
bands. A user-defined environment can be
passed as a matrix with values in $[0, 1]$ (`airmat`).

## Speciation mechanisms

The default speciation mechanism is point speciation: in each generation, the
number of new species is drawn from a Poisson distribution with mean
`specRate`, and for each of them an individual is chosen at random. `specRate`
is thus the expected number of new species per generation in the whole grid,
not a rate per individual. The founding individual keeps its traits, which
become the initial trait means of the new species (see Known limitations).

All speciation mechanisms implemented in the model are summarized below:

- **Point speciation:** the default, see above.
- **Fission type 1:** an individual is drawn at random, so that species are
  chosen in proportion to their abundance; every second individual of its
  species becomes part of a new species.
- **Fission type 2:** as type 1, but the species is split geographically at the
  mean x-coordinate of its individuals. One part becomes a new species, the
  other part is not affected.
- **Protracted speciation:** based on @rosindell2010, a species undergoes an
  incipient stage before becoming a new species. In the implementation, the
  chosen individual becomes a new species only if it survives `protracted`
  generations; its offspring do not inherit the incipient state. `specRate` is
  then the expected number of incipient individuals per generation.
- **Red Queen:** based on @odwyer2014, new species have advantages over old
  species due to their novelty alone, and the effect vanishes over time. The
  fitness is multiplied by $1 + s \exp(-q\,a)$, where $s$ = `redQueenStrength`,
  $q$ = `redQueen` and $a$ is the number of generations since the species arose,
  minus one; without environment and density dependence, the base fitness is
  set to 0.01.

| Argument | Meaning | Default | Range |
|---|---|---|---|
| `specRate` | expected number of new species per generation in the whole grid | 1 | $\ge 0$, $\le x \cdot y$ |
| `fission` | speciation by fission: 0 (none), 1 or 2 | 0 | 0, 1, 2 |
| `protracted` | generations an incipient species must survive | 0 | integer $\ge 0$ |
| `redQueenStrength`, `redQueen` | strength $s$ and decay $q$ of the novelty advantage | 0, 0 | $\ge 0$ |

## Known limitations

::: {.limitation}
Some properties of the current implementation can be unexpected; they are
discussed in the issues of the package repository:

- `dispersal` has an effect only in steps of 0.5
  ([#141](https://github.com/TheoreticalEcology/EcoPhyloSim/issues/141)).
- With protracted speciation, the offspring of an incipient individual do not
  inherit the incipient state
  ([#143](https://github.com/TheoreticalEcology/EcoPhyloSim/issues/143)).
- New species keep the traits of their founding individual; a trait change at
  speciation is not implemented
  ([#114](https://github.com/TheoreticalEcology/EcoPhyloSim/issues/114)).
- Density dependence develops only after thousands of generations, so short
  runs show little of its effect
  ([#133](https://github.com/TheoreticalEcology/EcoPhyloSim/issues/133)).
- `es()` calculates the expected number of species of the neutral model with
  $\theta = 2 \cdot$ `specRate`, about twice the value that fits the model
  (see the chapter Emerging patterns;
  [#124](https://github.com/TheoreticalEcology/EcoPhyloSim/issues/124)).
:::

# Running the model

## Installation

The package is not on CRAN yet. Follow the instructions on
<https://github.com/TheoreticalEcology/EcoPhyloSim> to install the development
version, e.g.

```{r install, eval = FALSE}
devtools::install_github(repo = "TheoreticalEcology/EcoPhyloSim",
                         subdir = "PhyloSim",
                         dependencies = TRUE,
                         build_vignettes = TRUE)

?EcoPhyloSim
browseVignettes("EcoPhyloSim")
```

## Running a simulation

Running the model consists of two consecutive steps. First, a list of parameters
is generated with `createCompletePar()`:

```{r createpar}
pars <- createCompletePar(x = 50, y = 50, dispersal = "global", runs = c(500, 1000),
                          negativeDD = 1, environment = 0.5, specRate = 1, seed = 42)
```

In this example, an area of 50 × 50 cells provides the basis for one simulation
with outputs recorded after 500 and 1,000 generations. The dispersal is set to
global, meaning each individual could reproduce in every cell of the grid.
Further, both density dependence and the environment influence the
individuals. Besides the model parameters described above, `createCompletePar()`
has arguments that control the run and its output:

| Argument | Meaning | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `runs` | generation(s) at which the state is recorded; values must not decrease | 100 |
| `seed` | random seed; if `NULL`, a seed is drawn and stored in `$Model$seed` of the result | `NULL` |
| `prunePhylogeny` | if `TRUE`, the phylogeny contains only the extant species; if `FALSE`, also all extinct species as tips | `TRUE` |
| `convertToBinaryTree` | resolve polytomies of the phylogeny (deterministically, with `ape::multi2di(random = FALSE)`) | `TRUE` |
| `calculateSummaries` | calculate summary statistics (`calculateSummaryStatistics()`) for the last recorded generation | `FALSE` |
| `scenario` | a label stored with the parameters | `NULL` |

The list of parameters is then used to run the simulation:

```{r runsim, results = 'hide'}
simu <- runSimulation(pars)
```

This simulation took `r round(simu$Model$runtime, 1)` seconds. Note that 1,000
generations are enough for a first look, but some outputs, in particular with
density dependence and the phylogeny, need several thousand generations to
reach equilibrium (see the section on the time to equilibrium below).

The result is an object of class `PhyloSim` with two lists: `$Model` contains
the parameters of the run, and `$Output` contains one element per generation
in `runs`, here two. Each of them contains:

| Element | Content |
|---|---|
| `specMat` | species of each cell (matrix with $y$ rows and $x$ columns) |
| `traitMat`, `compMat`, `neutMat` | environmental, competition and neutral trait of each cell |
| `envMat` | environment of each cell |
| `phylogeny` | phylogeny of the species (class `phylo` of the package ape; 0 if only one species is left) |
| `phyloTXT` | the phylogeny as Newick text |
| `summaries` | summary statistics if `calculateSummaries = TRUE`, stored in the first element of `$Output` only |

```{r output1}
str(simu$Output[[1]], max.level = 1)
```

Branch lengths of the phylogeny are in generations, with each recorded state
placed half a generation after the events of its generation (see
`?runSimulation`).

The `PhyloSim` object serves as the basis of all further analysis. It can
directly be passed to all other functions. If the `PhyloSim` object contains
multiple results, they can be accessed by the `which.result` argument in most
functions. By default, the last result is used.

## Several simulations

Often, users will want to run several simulations with different or equal
parameters. For this purpose, the `runSimulationBatch()` function runs a list
of parameter combinations, optionally in parallel, and returns an object of
class `PhylosimList`, which is essentially a list of `PhyloSim` objects. In the
following example, two slightly different parameter sets are run one after
the other; for larger batches, `parallel = 2` runs them on two cores.

```{r runbatch, results = 'hide'}
pars1 <- createCompletePar(x = 50, y = 50, dispersal = "global", runs = 1000,
                           negativeDD = 1, environment = 0.5, specRate = 1, seed = 1)
pars2 <- createCompletePar(x = 50, y = 50, dispersal = "global", runs = 1000,
                           negativeDD = 1, environment = 1, specRate = 1, seed = 2)
simuBatch <- runSimulationBatch(list(pars1, pars2), parallel = FALSE)
```

The single simulations can be accessed by indexing, e.g. `simuBatch[[1]]`. An
overview of the basic classes and functions to run simulations is provided
below.

```{r runfig, echo = FALSE, out.width = "80%", fig.cap = "Overview of the basic model functions in the EcoPhyloSim package. Functions are represented by bubbles, objects by circles. Objects of the class PhylosimList can be indexed if a single PhyloSim object is needed."}
knitr::include_graphics("runsimulation.svg")
```

# Plots and summary statistics

This chapter explains the functions that plot and summarize the output of a
simulation. All of them take a `PhyloSim` object and use its last recorded
generation unless `which.result` is given, except `getMortalityData()`, which
uses all recorded generations; some also accept a `PhylosimList`.
The table gives an overview.

| Function | Shows or returns | Typical question |
|---|---|---|
| `plotSpatialPhylo()` | phylogeny, mean traits and map of the species | Which species live where, and how are they related? |
| `plotTraitDistribution()` | traits against the environment, in space and per species | Do traits match the environment? Are competition traits spread out? |
| `sac()` | species–area curve | How fast do species accumulate with the sampled area? |
| `rac()` | rank–abundance curve | How even are the abundances? |
| `phyloReconstruct()` | tree clustered from the neutral traits | How much does trait similarity tell about relatedness? |
| `highlightLocalPhylo()` | species of a subplot in the tree of the whole grid | Are the species of a local community related? |
| `specRich()`, `collessImbalance()` | single statistics | How many species? How balanced is the tree? |
| `calculateSummaryStatistics()` | a set of statistics | Summaries for comparisons and calibration |
| `localPlots()` | random subplots (an observation model) | What would a field survey see? |
| `getMortalityData()` | death and conspecific neighbors of each individual | How strong is conspecific density dependence? |
| `nullModel()`, `calculatePhylogeneticDispersion()` | phylogenetic dispersion against random communities | Are local communities phylogenetically clustered or overdispersed? |

## Plot functions

**`plotSpatialPhylo()`** is the default plot method for a `PhyloSim` object and
gives a first overview of a simulation. Each species has the same color in the
phylogeny and in the map, and related species have similar colors; the middle
panel shows the mean environment and traits of the species (point size), in
the order of the tips. *How to read it:* in the map, patches of one color show
spatial aggregation, which local dispersal creates even in the neutral model;
colors that follow the environmental gradient show environmental filtering. The
middle panel shows whether related species have similar traits.

```{r plotspatialphylo, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5, fig.cap = "Phylogeny of the species (left), their mean traits (middle; point size) and their spatial distribution (right), with colors matching the colors in the phylogeny. The arguments plot and plotTraits select the panels."}
plotSpatialPhylo(simu)
```

**Species–area curve:** `sac()` computes the mean number of species in square
subplots of increasing size, placed at random in the grid. *How to read it:* on
log–log axes, the slope tells how fast new species appear with area. Spatial
aggregation (local dispersal) makes small subplots poor in species and the
curve steep; with global dispersal, subplots are close to random samples of the
whole grid and the curve flattens early.

```{r sac, results = 'hide', fig.width = 5, fig.height = 5, fig.cap = "Species–area curve: mean number of species against the area of the subplots (both axes logarithmic). Its shape depends on dispersal and spatial aggregation (see the chapter Emerging patterns)."}
sac(simu)
```

**Rank–abundance curve:** `rac()` shows the abundance of each species in the
whole grid against its rank. *How to read it:* a steep curve means that a few
species dominate, a flat one that abundances are even; the length of the curve
is the number of species. Density dependence is expected to flatten the curve,
as it favors rare species.

```{r rac, results = 'hide', fig.width = 5, fig.height = 5, fig.cap = "Rank–abundance curve: abundance of each species against its rank (most abundant species = rank 1). The chapter Emerging patterns compares such curves with the expectation of neutral theory."}
rac(simu)
```

**Trait plots:** `plotTraitDistribution()` shows the three traits of the
individuals. *How to read it:* with environmental filtering, the environmental
trait follows the environment (points along the diagonal in the top panel);
with density dependence, the competition traits of neighbors differ, and they
can move to the ends of the trait range (see Density dependence in the chapter
Emerging patterns). The neutral trait changes only by drift and serves as a
reference.

```{r traitdist, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 6, fig.cap = "Environmental, competition and neutral trait (columns): trait against the environment of the cell (top), spatial distribution (middle) and histograms per species (bottom; colors as in plotSpatialPhylo)."}
plotTraitDistribution(simu, type = "all")
```

**Reconstructed phylogenies:** `phyloReconstruct()` clusters the species by the
mean of their neutral trait (hierarchical clustering with `hclust()`). As the
neutral trait changes only by drift, comparing the result with the true
phylogeny shows how much phylogenetic signal such a trait carries.

```{r phylorecon, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4, fig.cap = "Phylogeny reconstructed from the mean neutral traits of the species (left) and the true phylogeny of the extant species (right)."}
reconstructed <- phyloReconstruct(simu)
true <- simu$Output[[length(simu$Output)]]$phylogeny

op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(reconstructed, main = "Reconstructed phylogeny")
plot(true, main = "True phylogeny")
par(op)
```

**Highlight local communities:** `highlightLocalPhylo()` highlights the species
of a local community, a randomly placed subplot, in the phylogeny of the whole
grid (the metacommunity). *How to read it:* highlighted species that sit in a
few clades indicate phylogenetic clustering, species spread over the whole tree
overdispersion; the null models below test this.

```{r highlight-large, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 5.4, fig.cap = "Species of a subplot of 10 × 10 cells (highlighted) in the phylogeny of the metacommunity."}
highlightLocalPhylo(simu, size = 10, n = 1)
```

```{r highlight-small, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 5.4, fig.cap = "Species of a subplot of 5 × 5 cells (highlighted) in the phylogeny of the metacommunity."}
highlightLocalPhylo(simu, size = 5, n = 1)
```

The larger subplot contains more species than the smaller one.

## Summary statistics

Single statistics of a simulation can be calculated directly, e.g. the number
of species and the Yule-normalized Colless index of the phylogeny (about 0 for
a tree as balanced as expected under a Yule process, positive for more
imbalanced trees):

```{r stats}
specRich(simu)
collessImbalance(simu, norm = "yule")
```

`calculateSummaryStatistics()` computes a set of statistics at once, e.g. to
compare simulations or to fit the model to data (see the chapter Fitting the
model to data). It takes some seconds, as the phylogenetic dispersion is
computed with a null model; with `calculateSummaries = TRUE` in
`createCompletePar()`, `runSimulation()` computes them for the last recorded
generation.

```{r summarystats, eval = FALSE}
calculateSummaryStatistics(simu)
```

| Group | Statistic | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| Diversity | `gammaDiversity`, `alphaDiversity`, `betaDiversity` | species in the grid, mean species in subplots, turnover between subplots |
| Abundances and space | `racAuc`, `sacAuc` | area under the rank–abundance and species–area curves |
| | `ce`, `nb8` | spatial aggregation of the species: mean Clark–Evans index over the species, and an index of conspecifics among the 8 neighboring cells |
| Traits and environment | `envSorting` | share of the variance of the environment explained by species identity (0 if all species occupy the same mix of environments, 1 if each species occupies one environment; see `?calculateSummaryStatistics`) |
| | `varPart_1`, `varPart_2` | variance of the community composition explained by environment and by competition traits |
| Phylogeny | `imbalance`, `gammaStatistics` | Colless index and gamma statistic (negative: branching slows down towards the present) |
| | `meanNodeAge`, `dispersion` | mean branch length; standardized phylogenetic dispersion of subplots (SES of the MPD) |

The phylogenetic statistics use the tree of the extant species. Several
statistics use random subplots; call `set.seed()` first for reproducible values
(`?calculateSummaryStatistics` gives the details).

Several functions, such as species–area curves and the null models below, are
based on `localPlots()`, a simple observation model that creates random
subplots of a given size within the metacommunity and returns their species,
environment and competition traits and positions:

```{r localplots}
str(localPlots(simu, size = 10, n = 2), max.level = 1)
```

**Mortality data:** `getMortalityData()` returns, for each individual, the number
of its conspecific neighbors and whether it died until the next recorded
generation, which allows estimating conspecific negative density dependence
as in field studies (see the section Density dependence measured from
mortality). For this, the state
should be recorded in consecutive generations:

```{r mortality-run, results = 'hide'}
simuM <- runSimulation(createCompletePar(x = 30, y = 30, dispersal = 1, negativeDD = 1,
                                         runs = c(4000, 4001), seed = 3))
```

```{r mortality}
mort <- getMortalityData(simuM)
head(mort)
```

## Null models

Phylogenetic patterns of local communities are only meaningful against what
random communities would show. `nullModel()` places subplots in the
metacommunity and compares their mean pairwise phylogenetic distance (MPD) with
that of random communities of the same size, drawn from the abundances of the
species in the whole grid (`abundance = FALSE`, the default) or in all sampled
subplots together (`abundance = TRUE`):

```{r nullmodel}
pValues <- nullModel(simu = simu, abundance = FALSE, localPlotSize = 10,
                     numberOfPlots = 20, repetitions = 100, fun = "mpd")
round(pValues, 2)
```

Each value is the share of random communities whose MPD is at most the
observed one. Small values mean that the species of a subplot are more closely
related than expected by chance (phylogenetic clustering), large values that
they are less closely related (phylogenetic overdispersion). Such p-values, and
standardized effect sizes (SES) computed in the same way, depend on the size of
the subplots and on the null model (which species pool, whether abundances are
used); compare only values computed with the same settings.

**`calculatePhylogeneticDispersion()`:** this and its associated plot function
are convenience functions for a rather specialized application: they calculate
null models for all runs in a `PhylosimList` object and for different plot
sizes. Which null model is used is determined by the `type` argument:

- `"PhylMeta"`: equivalent to `nullModel()` with `abundance = FALSE`.
- `"PhylSample"`: equivalent to `nullModel()` with `abundance = TRUE`.
- `"PhylPool"`: uses `picante::ses.mpd()` with `null.model = "phylogeny.pool"`.
- `"SamplePool"`: uses `picante::ses.mpd()` with `null.model = "sample.pool"`.

```{r calcphyldis, eval = FALSE}
pValuesBatch <- calculatePhylogeneticDispersion(simuBatch, plotlengths = 3,
                                                plots = 20, replicates = 20,
                                                type = "PhylMeta")
```

The result can be visualized with `plotPhylogeneticDispersion()`. The figure
uses example results stored in the package (`pPD.pvalues`, `pPD.positions`);
they illustrate the plot only.

```{r plotphyldis, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 5, fig.cap = "Phylogenetic dispersion for combinations of dispersal limitation (rows), environmental filtering (upper axis) and density dependence (lower axis). The color shows whether the local communities are phylogenetically clustered or overdispersed."}
data("pPD.pvalues")
data("pPD.positions")

plotPhylogeneticDispersion(pvalues = pPD.pvalues, positions = pPD.positions,
                           title = "Null Meta")
```

# Emerging patterns

This chapter shows how the main outputs of the model respond to its
parameters, and compares them with what theory and earlier studies lead us to
expect. For the neutral model, some expectations are exact analytical
results; for the other processes, the literature mostly predicts the direction
of an effect. The parameters are varied one or two at a time around a reference
setting (50 × 50 cells, `dispersal = 1`, `specRate = 2`, all other parameters
at their defaults), with replicate runs per setting. The simulations take
hours to days, so they are not run when this vignette is built: they were run
with the script `data-raw/packageBehavior.R` in the
[package repository](https://github.com/TheoreticalEcology/EcoPhyloSim), and
their summaries are stored in the data set `packageBehavior` (see
`?packageBehavior`). They were run with an earlier version of the package
(commit
`r packageBehavior$info$commit`), in which
polytomies of the phylogeny were resolved at random
([#174](https://github.com/TheoreticalEcology/EcoPhyloSim/pull/174)); with the
current version, the Colless index would differ slightly. Results with density
dependence differ more in the current version, which redesigned density
dependence
([#172](https://github.com/TheoreticalEcology/EcoPhyloSim/pull/172)); the runs
use the earlier parameter names `density` and `densityCut` (now `negativeDD` and
`negativeDDCut`). How these patterns changed between releases is shown in the
vignette "Model history" (`vignette("ModelHistory", package = "EcoPhyloSim")`).

The indicators are computed for the whole grid at each census: species
richness, Shannon diversity, the share of the four neighbors of a cell that
belong to the same species (spatial aggregation), the correlation between the
environmental trait and the environment, the standard deviation of the
competition trait, and the Yule-normalized Colless index and the gamma
statistic of the tree of the extant species. The table summarizes the
expectations that the following sections test.

| Process | Expectation | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Grid size | richness increases with the number of individuals, faster with local dispersal | @ewens1972, @durrett1996 |
| Neutral model, global dispersal | richness and abundance distribution as in the Ewens sampling formula with $\theta \approx$ `specRate`; share of conspecific neighbors $1/(1+\theta)$ | @ewens1972, @vallade2003 |
| Neutral model | tree more imbalanced than a Yule tree (Colless index > 0); species old, abundant species older | @davies2011, @manceau2015, @chisholm2014 |
| Protracted speciation | fewer species | @rosindell2010, see below |
| Red Queen | younger species | @odwyer2014 |
| Dispersal limitation | spatial clusters of conspecifics; similarity decreasing with distance; steeper species–area curves within the grid | @durrett1996, @rosindell2007, @chave2002, @chaveleigh2002 |
| Environmental filtering | traits match the environment, more so with local dispersal; effect on richness can be positive or negative | @mouquet2003, @stein2014, @allouche2012 |
| Strength of selection | effects of environment and density dependence increase with `fitnessBaseMortalityRatio`; neutral at 1 | model definition |
| Density dependence | more species, more even abundances, fewer conspecific neighbors, more dispersed competition traits | @chave2002, @levi2019, @scheffer2006 |
| Environment and density dependence | effects can mask each other; in the runs of this chapter (before #172), neutral if both are > 0 and their sum is ≤ 1 | @kraft2015 |
| Assembly processes and dispersal | environmental filtering increases, density dependence reduces aggregation; both increase richness; dispersal changes how strongly each shows | @kraft2015, @mouquet2003, @adler2005 |
| Niche width | richness possibly highest at an intermediate width; best match of traits and environment for narrow niches | @allouche2012 |
| CNDD from mortality | coefficient close to 0 without and positive with density dependence; per-species estimates biased towards stronger CNDD of rare species | @comita2010, @hulsmann2024, @detto2019 |

```{css, echo = FALSE}
.expectation {
  background-color: #f2f6fa;
  border-left: 4px solid #0072B2;
  padding: 0.4em 1em;
  margin: 1em 0;
}
.limitation {
  background-color: #fbf3ec;
  border-left: 4px solid #D55E00;
  padding: 0.4em 1em;
  margin: 1em 0;
}
```

```{r patterns-setup, echo = FALSE}
data("packageBehavior")
pilot <- packageBehavior$pilot
main <- packageBehavior$main

labels <- c(richness = "Species richness", shannon = "Shannon diversity",
            conspecificNeighbors = "Conspecific neighbors",
            corTraitEnv = "Cor(trait, env.)",
            sdCompetitionTrait = "SD comp. trait",
            colless = "Colless index", gamma = "Gamma statistic")
# colorblind-safe palette (Okabe & Ito)
cols <- c("#0072B2", "#D55E00", "#009E73", "#CC79A7", "#E69F00", "#56B4E9")

# common style of all figures in this chapter (set for each chunk by the hook)
style <- function(...) par(mar = c(3.4, 3.4, 1.6, 0.6), mgp = c(2.1, 0.55, 0), tcl = -0.3,
                           las = 1, bty = "l", cex = 0.75, font.main = 1, cex.main = 1, ...)
knitr::knit_hooks$set(style = function(before, options, envir) if (before) style())
knitr::opts_chunk$set(style = TRUE, fig.retina = 2)

# x axis with plain numbers (no scientific notation) on a log scale
logAxis <- function(side = 1) {
  at <- axTicks(side)
  axis(side, at = at, labels = format(at, big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE, trim = TRUE))
}

# legend in an empty panel of a multi-panel figure
legendPanel <- function(...) {
  plot.new()
  legend("center", bty = "n", cex = 0.95, ...)
}

# 95% confidence intervals as error bars
ciBars <- function(x, m, ci, col) {
  # skip intervals too short to draw (they give "zero-length arrow" warnings)
  ok <- is.finite(ci) & ci > 1e-3 * diff(par("usr")[3:4])
  arrows(x[ok], m[ok] - ci[ok], x[ok], m[ok] + ci[ok], angle = 90, code = 3,
         length = 0.02, col = col)
}

# setting number of a block with the given parameter values
settingId <- function(d, block, ...) {
  s <- d$settings[d$settings$block == block, ]
  v <- list(...)
  for (n in names(v)) s <- s[s[[n]] == v[[n]], ]
  s$setting
}

# replicate mean and 95% confidence interval at the last census of each setting
final <- function(d, block, indicator) {
  x <- d$census[d$census$block == block & d$census$indicator == indicator, ]
  x <- x[x$generation == ave(x$generation, x$setting, FUN = max), ]
  x$ci <- qt(0.975, pmax(x$n - 1, 1)) * x$sd / sqrt(x$n)
  merge(d$settings[d$settings$block == block, ], x[c("setting", "mean", "ci", "n")])
}

# indicators against a parameter (x-axis), one line per value of `group`
response <- function(d, block, xvar, group = NULL, indicators = names(labels),
                     xlab = xvar, log = "", settings = NULL) {
  op <- style(mfrow = c(2, ceiling((length(indicators) + 1) / 2)))
  on.exit(par(op))
  for (ind in indicators) {
    f <- final(d, block, ind)
    if (!is.null(settings)) f <- f[f$setting %in% settings, ]
    f <- f[order(f$setting), ]
    xv <- f[[xvar]]
    isFactor <- is.character(xv)
    if (isFactor) xv <- match(xv, unique(xv))
    g <- if (is.null(group)) rep("", nrow(f)) else as.character(f[[group]])
    yr <- range(c(f$mean - f$ci, f$mean + f$ci), na.rm = TRUE)
    if (!all(is.finite(yr))) yr <- c(0, 1)
    plot(xv, f$mean, type = "n", ylim = yr, xlab = xlab, ylab = "", main = labels[ind],
         log = log, xaxt = "n")
    if (isFactor) axis(1, at = seq_along(unique(f[[xvar]])), labels = unique(f[[xvar]]), gap.axis = 0)
    else if (grepl("x", log)) logAxis(1) else axis(1)
    for (k in seq_along(unique(g))) {
      sel <- g == unique(g)[k]
      lines(xv[sel], f$mean[sel], col = cols[k], type = "b", pch = 16)
      ciBars(xv[sel], f$mean[sel], f$ci[sel], cols[k])
    }
  }
  if (!is.null(group))
    legendPanel(legend = unique(g), col = cols[seq_along(unique(g))], lty = 1, pch = 16,
                title = group)
}

# replicate mean (line) and mean +/- sd (band) of each indicator over time
trajectories <- function(d, cases, indicators = names(labels)) {
  op <- style(mfrow = c(2, ceiling((length(indicators) + 1) / 2)))
  on.exit(par(op))
  for (ind in indicators) {
    x <- d$census[d$census$indicator == ind, ]
    sub <- lapply(seq_len(nrow(cases)), function(k)
      x[x$block == cases$block[k] & x$setting == cases$setting[k], ])
    yr <- range(unlist(lapply(sub, function(s) c(s$mean - s$sd, s$mean + s$sd))), na.rm = TRUE)
    plot(1, type = "n", log = "x", xlim = range(x$generation), ylim = yr,
         xlab = "Generation", ylab = "", main = labels[ind], xaxt = "n")
    logAxis(1)
    for (k in seq_along(sub)) {
      s <- sub[[k]][order(sub[[k]]$generation), ]
      ok <- is.finite(s$sd)
      polygon(c(s$generation[ok], rev(s$generation[ok])),
              c(s$mean[ok] - s$sd[ok], rev(s$mean[ok] + s$sd[ok])),
              col = adjustcolor(cols[k], 0.25), border = NA)
      lines(s$generation, s$mean, col = cols[k])
    }
  }
  legendPanel(legend = cases$label, col = cols[seq_len(nrow(cases))], lwd = 2)
}

# neutral theory for J individuals and specRate new species per generation:
# speciation probability per replacement nu = specRate / J and
# theta = (J - 1) nu / (1 - nu) (Vallade & Houchmandzadeh 2003, eq. 6)
theta <- function(specRate, J) (J - 1) * (specRate / J) / (1 - specRate / J)
# expected species richness (Ewens sampling formula)
ewens <- function(theta, J) sum(theta / (theta + 0:(J - 1)))
# expected rank-abundance curve: mean of sorted abundances of random
# Ewens partitions (Hoppe urn); like the simulated curves, each rank is
# averaged over the partitions that have at least that many species
ewensRac <- function(theta, J, reps = 200) {
  racs <- replicate(reps, {
    sp <- integer(J)
    n <- 0
    for (i in seq_len(J)) {
      if (runif(1) < theta / (theta + i - 1)) {
        n <- n + 1
        sp[i] <- n
      } else sp[i] <- sp[sample.int(i - 1, 1)]
    }
    sort(tabulate(sp), decreasing = TRUE)
  }, simplify = FALSE)
  len <- max(lengths(racs))
  rowMeans(sapply(racs, function(r) c(r, rep(NA, len - length(r)))), na.rm = TRUE)
}
# replicate mean of an indicator at the last census, for the setting of a block
# with the given parameter values (for the text)
val <- function(block, indicator, ..., digits = 2) {
  f <- final(main, block, indicator)
  signif(f$mean[f$setting == settingId(main, block, ...)], digits)
}
```

## Run length and runtime

This part shows how long a simulation must run to reach equilibrium and how
long it takes.

### Time to equilibrium

All results below refer to the state of the model at the end of the runs. In
the main runs, each setting was simulated
`r packageBehavior$info$modes$main$reps` times for
`r format(packageBehavior$info$modes$main$generations[["default"]], big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE)`
generations
(`r format(packageBehavior$info$modes$main$generations[["density"]], big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE)`
in the density block,
`r format(packageBehavior$info$modes$main$generations[["neutral"]], big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE)`
in the neutral block).

::: {.expectation}
**Expectation.** In the neutral model, abundances change only by drift, which
is slower in larger communities. We therefore expect the time to equilibrium
to grow with the number of cells, and to be longer for indicators that depend
on the whole history of the community (the phylogeny) than for those that
depend on the current abundances.
:::

To check how long the model needs to reach equilibrium, a pilot run simulated
each setting for
`r format(packageBehavior$info$modes$pilot$generations[["default"]], big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE)`
generations
(`r format(packageBehavior$info$modes$pilot$generations[["density"]], big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE)`
in the density block) with
`r packageBehavior$info$modes$pilot$reps` replicates. The figure shows the
replicate mean (line) and the variation between replicates (band: mean ± sd)
of each indicator over time for five settings. Most diversity and spatial
indicators settle within a few thousand generations, except richness on large
grids. The gamma statistic and the spread of the competition trait settle much
more slowly in many settings, also in the neutral model, often only after
20,000 generations or more; with 5 replicates, this criterion is also noisy.
The results for these indicators therefore describe a slowly changing rather
than a fully stationary state.

```{r equilibrium, echo = FALSE, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5, fig.cap = "Indicators over time in the pilot runs: replicate mean (line) and mean ± standard deviation across replicates (band)."}
cases <- data.frame(
  block = c("neutral", "neutral", "dispersal", "environment", "density"),
  setting = c(settingId(pilot, "neutral", specRate = 2, x = 50),
              settingId(pilot, "neutral", specRate = 0.5, x = 100),
              settingId(pilot, "dispersal", dispersal = "1"),
              settingId(pilot, "environment", environment = 1, dispersal = "1"),
              settingId(pilot, "density", density = 1, densityCut = 1)),
  label = c("neutral, global", "neutral, global,\n100 x 100,\nspecRate 0.5",
            "neutral, dispersal 1", "environment 1", "density 1"))
trajectories(pilot, cases)
```

The table gives, for the same settings, the first census after which the
replicate mean of an indicator stays within 5% of its final level (the mean
over the last quarter of the run) or within its 95% confidence interval,
whichever is wider.

```{r equilibrium-table, echo = FALSE}
eqTime <- function(d, block, setting, indicator) {
  x <- d$census[d$census$block == block & d$census$setting == setting &
                  d$census$indicator == indicator, ]
  x <- x[order(x$generation), ]
  last <- x$generation >= 0.75 * max(x$generation)
  level <- mean(x$mean[last])
  tol <- max(0.05 * abs(level), mean(qt(0.975, x$n[last] - 1) * x$sd[last] / sqrt(x$n[last])))
  out <- which(is.na(x$mean) | abs(x$mean - level) > tol)
  if (length(out) == 0) return(format(min(x$generation), big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE))
  if (max(out) == nrow(x)) return("not reached")
  format(x$generation[max(out) + 1], big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE)
}
tab <- sapply(seq_len(nrow(cases)), function(k)
  sapply(names(labels), eqTime, d = pilot, block = cases$block[k], setting = cases$setting[k]))
dimnames(tab) <- list(labels, gsub("\n", " ", cases$label))
knitr::kable(tab, caption = "Generations to equilibrium in the pilot runs.")
```

### Runtime

```{r runtime-setup, echo = FALSE}
# runtimes of the runs of this chapter, stored in modelHistory (built with
# model-behavior/makeData.R; missing in installations without it)
hasRuntime <- exists("modelHistory") ||
  "modelHistory" %in% utils::data(package = "EcoPhyloSim")$results[, "Item"]
if (hasRuntime && !exists("modelHistory")) data("modelHistory")
rt <- if (hasRuntime) modelHistory$summary else data.frame(indicator = character(0), version = character(0),
                                                           block = character(0), mean = numeric(0), generations = numeric(0))
rt <- rt[rt$indicator == "runtime" & rt$version == "0.3.1", ]
rt$per1000 <- rt$mean / rt$generations * 1000
# runtime per 1,000 generations of the setting of a block with the given parameter values
rtVal <- function(block, ..., digits = 2) {
  d <- rt[rt$block == block, ]
  v <- list(...)
  for (n in names(v)) d <- d[d[[n]] == v[[n]], ]
  if (!nrow(d)) return(NA)
  signif(d$per1000, digits)
}
```

::: {.expectation}
**Expectation.** In each generation, every individual dies and is replaced, so
the runtime grows with the number of cells. Each replacement looks at the
cells within the dispersal kernel and, with density dependence, at the
neighborhood of the recruit, so larger kernels and neighborhoods take longer.
:::

The figure shows the runtime of the core simulation per 1,000 generations in
the runs of this chapter (replicate means; one core of a desktop PC, 10
simulations in parallel; the runtimes of these runs are stored in the data set
`modelHistory`). Runtimes on other computers and in the current version
differ, but
the ratios between settings should be similar. On 50 × 50 cells, global
dispersal is fastest (`r rtVal("dispersal", dispersal = "global")` seconds per
1,000 generations). With local dispersal, the runtime increases steeply with
the dispersal distance (from `r rtVal("dispersal", dispersal = "0.5")` seconds
at 0.5 to `r rtVal("dispersal", dispersal = "3")` seconds at 3). With dispersal 1,
it grows somewhat faster than the number of cells. Density dependence increases it up to about
`r round(max(rtVal("density", densityCut = 1)) / rtVal("density", density = 0, densityCut = 1))`-fold
with neighborhood radius 1 and
`r round(max(rtVal("density", densityCut = 2)) / rtVal("density", density = 0, densityCut = 2))`-fold
with radius 2. Together with the time to equilibrium, this gives the cost of a
simulation: e.g. 50,000 generations on 100 × 100 cells with dispersal 1 take
about `r round(rtVal("gridSize", x = 100) * 50 / 60)` minutes.

```{r runtime, echo = FALSE, eval = hasRuntime, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 2.6, fig.cap = "Runtime of the core simulation in seconds per 1,000 generations against the dispersal kernel (50 × 50 cells), the number of cells (dispersal 1) and the strength of density dependence (dispersal 1, two neighborhood radii)."}
op <- style(mfrow = c(1, 3))
d <- rt[rt$block == "dispersal", ]
d <- d[match(c("global", "0.5", "1", "2", "3"), d$dispersal), ]
plot(seq_len(nrow(d)), d$per1000, type = "b", pch = 16, col = cols[1], xaxt = "n",
     xlab = "Dispersal", ylab = "Seconds per 1,000 generations", main = "Dispersal")
axis(1, at = seq_len(nrow(d)), labels = d$dispersal)
d <- rt[rt$block == "gridSize", ]
d <- d[order(d$x), ]
plot(d$x^2, d$per1000, type = "b", pch = 16, col = cols[1], log = "xy", xaxt = "n",
     xlab = "Cells", ylab = "", main = "Grid size")
axis(1, at = d$x^2, labels = format(d$x^2, big.mark = ","))
d <- rt[rt$block == "density", ]
plot(range(d$density), range(d$per1000), type = "n", xlab = "Density dependence",
     ylab = "", main = "Density dependence")
for (k in 1:2) {
  dk <- d[d$densityCut == k, ]
  dk <- dk[order(dk$density), ]
  lines(dk$density, dk$per1000, type = "b", pch = 16, col = cols[k])
}
legend("topleft", legend = paste("densityCut", 1:2), col = cols[1:2], lty = 1, pch = 16, bty = "n")
par(op)
```

## Neutral model and speciation

This part shows the neutral model, the reference for all other processes, the
speciation mechanisms and the effect of the grid size.

### Neutral model and speciation rate

::: {.expectation}
**Expectation.** With global dispersal and no fitness differences, the model
is a zero-sum Moran model: in each generation, $J = x \cdot y$ individuals die
and are replaced by offspring of random individuals, and on average `specRate`
of the replacements found a new species, so the speciation probability per
replacement is $\nu = \texttt{specRate}/J$. (In `runSimulation()`, the new
species arise at the end of each generation rather than at single
replacements, so the model is close to, but not exactly, a Moran model.) The
equilibrium of the Moran model is known exactly [@vallade2003]. The number of
species follows the Ewens sampling formula [@ewens1972],
$$E(S) = \sum_{i=0}^{J-1} \frac{\theta}{\theta + i}, \qquad
\theta = \frac{(J-1)\,\nu}{1-\nu} \approx \texttt{specRate}.$$
For large $J$ and small $\nu$, this $\theta$ is about half of the fundamental
biodiversity number $2J\nu$ used in other formulations of neutral theory
[@hubbell2001; @vallade2003]; `es()` uses $2J\nu$ (see Known limitations). The
same theory predicts that two random individuals belong to the same species
with probability $1/(1+\theta)$. With global dispersal, space plays no role, so
this is also the expected share of conspecific neighbors. The theory also gives
the expected abundance distribution [@vallade2003], which we compare with the
rank–abundance curve of the model.

For the tree of the extant species, neutral theory predicts more imbalance
than a Yule tree, because the speciation probability of a species is
proportional to its abundance [@davies2011; @manceau2015]. The
Yule-normalized Colless index is close to 0 for Yule trees [@blum2006], so we
expect positive values. Neutral models in equilibrium are not expected to show
the slowdown of branching towards the present (negative gamma statistic) that
is typical of empirical trees [@davies2011; @manceau2015; @phillimore2008].
:::

```{r neutral, echo = FALSE, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 3.5, fig.cap = "Neutral model with global dispersal against the speciation rate, for three grid sizes (replicate mean and 95% confidence interval). Left: species richness; dashed: Ewens sampling formula, dotted: es(). Right: share of conspecific neighbors; dashed: 1/(1 + θ)."}
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
f <- final(main, "neutral", "richness")
g <- final(main, "neutral", "conspecificNeighbors")
sizes <- sort(unique(f$x))
sr <- exp(seq(log(min(f$specRate)), log(max(f$specRate)), length.out = 30))
plot(f$specRate, f$mean, type = "n", log = "xy", xlab = "specRate",
     ylab = "Species richness", ylim = range(c(pmax(f$mean - f$ci, 1), 2 * f$mean), na.rm = TRUE))
for (k in seq_along(sizes)) {
  s <- f[f$x == sizes[k], ]
  points(s$specRate, s$mean, col = cols[k], pch = 16)
  ciBars(s$specRate, s$mean, s$ci, cols[k])
  lines(sr, sapply(sr, function(r) ewens(theta(r, sizes[k]^2), sizes[k]^2)), col = cols[k], lty = 2)
  lines(sr, sapply(sr, es, dimensions = sizes[k]), col = cols[k], lty = 3)
}
legend("topleft", legend = paste(sizes, "x", sizes), col = cols[seq_along(sizes)],
       pch = 16, bty = "n")
plot(g$specRate, g$mean, type = "n", log = "x", xlab = "specRate",
     ylab = "Conspecific neighbors", ylim = c(0, 1))
for (k in seq_along(sizes)) {
  s <- g[g$x == sizes[k], ]
  points(s$specRate, s$mean, col = cols[k], pch = 16)
  ciBars(s$specRate, s$mean, s$ci, cols[k])
  lines(sr, 1 / (1 + theta(sr, sizes[k]^2)), col = cols[k], lty = 2)
}
par(op)
```

```{r neutral-rac, echo = FALSE, fig.width = 4.5, fig.height = 4, fig.cap = "Rank–abundance curve of the neutral model with global dispersal (50 × 50 cells, specRate = 2; replicate mean) and the expectation from the Ewens sampling formula (dashed)."}
s <- settingId(main, "neutral", specRate = 2, x = 50)
r <- main$rac[main$rac$block == "neutral" & main$rac$setting == s, ]
r <- r[order(r$rank), ]
set.seed(1)
e <- ewensRac(theta(2, 2500), 2500)
plot(r$rank, r$mean, log = "y", pch = 16, col = cols[1], xlab = "Rank",
     ylab = "Abundance", xlim = range(c(r$rank, seq_along(e))), ylim = c(0.5, max(r$mean, e)))
lines(seq_along(e)[e >= 0.5], e[e >= 0.5], lty = 2)
```

**Result.** The share of conspecific neighbors and the rank–abundance curve
agree with the Ewens sampling formula. Species richness is higher than expected
in all settings, by up to about 15%, but within the 95% confidence interval in
more than half of them (e.g.
`r val("neutral", "richness", x = 50, specRate = 8, digits = 3)` instead of
`r round(ewens(theta(8, 2500), 2500), 1)` for 50 × 50 cells and `specRate = 8`),
possibly because of the batch speciation described above
([#124](https://github.com/TheoreticalEcology/EcoPhyloSim/issues/124)). `es()`
gives 40–80% more species than the simulations, as expected from its definition
of $\theta$. As predicted, the Colless index is
positive in all settings. The gamma statistic is positive and increases with the
speciation rate, i.e. the trees show more recent than early branching.

### Protracted speciation and Red Queen

::: {.expectation}
**Expectation.** In the model, protracted speciation completes only if the
founding individual survives `protracted` generations (see Known limitations). An
individual survives a generation with probability of about $\exp(-1)$, so in the
neutral model protracted speciation should act like a speciation rate reduced
by a factor of about $\exp(-p)$, with $p$ = `protracted`, and richness should decrease accordingly. In
the original model of protracted speciation, in which the whole incipient
lineage becomes a new species [@rosindell2010], the effects are different;
there, protracted speciation also slows down branching towards the present
[@etienne2012]. A Red Queen advantage of young species is expected to make
species younger without changing abundance distributions much
[@odwyer2014]. Without environment and density dependence, the base fitness is
0.01, so `redQueenStrength` must be large (here 100) for young species to
survive the fitness-dependent draws noticeably more often.
:::

```{r protracted, echo = FALSE, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5, fig.cap = "Indicators against the duration of protracted speciation."}
response(main, "speciation", "protracted",
         settings = settingId(main, "speciation", redQueen = 0))
```

```{r protracted-ratio, echo = FALSE}
# richness relative to protracted = 0: simulated and Ewens with specRate * exp(-p)
rich <- function(p) val("speciation", "richness", protracted = p, redQueen = 0, digits = 10)
ewensRatio <- function(p) ewens(theta(2, 2500) * exp(-p), 2500) / ewens(theta(2, 2500), 2500)
```

**Result.** Richness decreases with `protracted` as predicted by a speciation
rate reduced by $\exp(-p)$: relative to `protracted = 0`, it is
`r round(rich(1) / rich(0), 2)` for $p = 1$ (Ewens sampling formula with the
reduced rate: `r round(ewensRatio(1), 2)`) and `r round(rich(2) / rich(0), 2)` for
$p = 2$ (`r round(ewensRatio(2), 2)`). With $p = 5$, most runs end with a single
species. The Red Queen advantage more than doubles richness
(`r val("speciation", "richness", redQueen = 0.01, digits = 3)` and
`r val("speciation", "richness", redQueen = 0.1, digits = 3)` species instead of
`r val("speciation", "richness", redQueen = 0, protracted = 0, digits = 3)`) and
strongly increases Shannon diversity, so it changes the abundance distribution
more than expected.

### Species ages

The age of a species is estimated from its ID: species are numbered in the
order of their origin, and new species arise at a roughly constant rate, so the
age of species $i$ at generation $G$ is about $G(1 - i/i_{max})$, where
$i_{max}$ is the largest ID in the phylogeny.

::: {.expectation}
**Expectation.** In neutral models, species persist for a long time, longer
than observed in nature [@chisholm2014], and since species start with one
individual and grow by drift, abundant species are on average older.
:::

```{r ages, echo = FALSE, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 3.5, fig.cap = "Mean species age (left) and rank correlation between age and abundance (right). Circles: neutral model with global dispersal against the speciation rate (50 × 50 cells). At specRate = 2, for dispersal = 1: without (square) and with a Red Queen advantage (triangles)."}
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
for (ind in c("meanSpeciesAge", "corAgeAbundance")) {
  f <- final(main, "neutral", ind)
  f <- f[f$x == 50, ]
  sp <- final(main, "speciation", ind)
  sp <- sp[sp$protracted == 0, ]
  sp <- sp[order(sp$redQueen), ]
  xs <- 2 * 1.12^(seq_len(nrow(sp)) - 1) # side by side at specRate = 2
  cs <- cols[1 + seq_len(nrow(sp))]
  yr <- range(c(f$mean - f$ci, f$mean + f$ci, sp$mean - sp$ci, sp$mean + sp$ci), na.rm = TRUE)
  plot(f$specRate, f$mean, log = "x", pch = 16, col = cols[1], ylim = yr, xlab = "specRate",
       xlim = range(c(f$specRate, xs)),
       ylab = if (ind == "meanSpeciesAge") "Mean species age (generations)" else "Cor(age, abundance)")
  ciBars(f$specRate, f$mean, f$ci, cols[1])
  points(xs, sp$mean, pch = ifelse(sp$redQueen > 0, 17, 15), col = cs)
  ciBars(xs, sp$mean, sp$ci, cs)
  if (ind == "meanSpeciesAge")
    legend("topright", legend = c("neutral, global", paste("dispersal 1, redQueen =", sp$redQueen)),
           pch = c(16, ifelse(sp$redQueen > 0, 17, 15)), col = c(cols[1], cs), bty = "n")
}
par(op)
```

**Result.** In the neutral model, mean species age decreases with the speciation
rate, and abundant species are older (rank correlation about
`r val("neutral", "corAgeAbundance", x = 50, specRate = 2, digits = 1)`), as
expected. The Red Queen advantage reduces the mean species age from
`r val("speciation", "meanSpeciesAge", redQueen = 0, protracted = 0, digits = 3)` to
about `r val("speciation", "meanSpeciesAge", redQueen = 0.01)` generations and
removes most of the correlation between age and abundance.

### Grid size

::: {.expectation}
**Expectation.** In the neutral model, richness increases roughly with the
logarithm of the number of individuals (Ewens sampling formula). With local
dispersal, larger grids also contain more spatially separated clusters
[@durrett1996], so richness should increase faster.
:::

```{r gridsize, echo = FALSE, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5, fig.cap = "Indicators against the grid size (cells per side) with local dispersal."}
response(main, "gridSize", "x", xlab = "grid size")
```

**Result.** With local dispersal, richness increases from
`r val("gridSize", "richness", x = 20, digits = 3)` to
`r val("gridSize", "richness", x = 100, digits = 3)` species between 20 × 20 and
100 × 100 cells, faster than in the neutral model with global dispersal (from
`r val("neutral", "richness", x = 20, specRate = 2, digits = 3)` to
`r val("neutral", "richness", x = 100, specRate = 2, digits = 3)`), as expected.

## Dispersal, environment and density dependence

This part shows the effects of dispersal, environmental filtering and density
dependence, alone and combined.

### Dispersal

::: {.expectation}
**Expectation.** With local dispersal, offspring settle near their parents, so
conspecifics form spatial clusters [@chaveleigh2002] and the share of
conspecific neighbors increases. Lineages in different parts of the grid stay
apart longer before they replace each other, so we expect more species on the
whole grid than with global dispersal. Species–area curves within a landscape
are steep at small areas when dispersal is short relative to the area
[@durrett1996; @rosindell2007], whereas global dispersal gives flatter curves
[@chave2002].
:::

```{r dispersal, echo = FALSE, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5, fig.cap = "Indicators against dispersal (replicate mean and 95% confidence interval)."}
response(main, "dispersal", "dispersal")
```

```{r dispersal-sac, echo = FALSE, fig.width = 4.5, fig.height = 4, fig.cap = "Species–area curves within the grid (mean number of species in square subplots of the given area) for different dispersal distances."}
s <- main$sac[main$sac$block == "dispersal", ]
st <- main$settings[main$settings$block == "dispersal", ]
plot(s$size, s$mean, type = "n", log = "xy", xlab = "Subplot area (cells)",
     ylab = "Species")
for (k in seq_len(nrow(st))) {
  x <- s[s$setting == st$setting[k], ]
  x <- x[order(x$size), ]
  lines(x$size, x$mean, col = cols[k], type = "b", pch = 16)
}
legend("topleft", legend = st$dispersal, col = cols[seq_len(nrow(st))], lty = 1,
       pch = 16, title = "dispersal", bty = "n")
```

The probability that two individuals at a given distance belong to the same
species is expected to decrease with distance when dispersal is limited
[@chaveleigh2002; @condit2002]. With global dispersal, it should be the same at
all distances and equal to the neutral expectation $1/(1+\theta)$.

```{r dispersal-decay, echo = FALSE, fig.width = 4.5, fig.height = 4, fig.cap = "Probability that two cells at the given distance (along rows and columns) contain the same species, for different dispersal distances (replicate mean and 95% confidence interval). Dashed: neutral expectation for global dispersal."}
s <- main$decay[main$decay$block == "dispersal", ]
s$ci <- qt(0.975, pmax(s$n - 1, 1)) * s$sd / sqrt(s$n)
plot(s$distance, s$mean, type = "n", log = "x", ylim = c(0, 1),
     xlab = "Distance (cells)", ylab = "Same species")
for (k in seq_len(nrow(st))) {
  x <- s[s$setting == st$setting[k], ]
  x <- x[order(x$distance), ]
  lines(x$distance, x$mean, col = cols[k], type = "b", pch = 16)
  ciBars(x$distance, x$mean, x$ci, cols[k])
}
abline(h = 1 / (1 + theta(2, 2500)), lty = 2)
legend("topright", legend = st$dispersal, col = cols[seq_len(nrow(st))], lty = 1,
       pch = 16, title = "dispersal", bty = "n")
```

**Result.** As expected, shorter dispersal increases richness on the whole grid
(`r val("dispersal", "richness", dispersal = "0.5", digits = 3)` species with
`dispersal = 0.5`, `r val("dispersal", "richness", dispersal = "global", digits = 3)`
with global dispersal) and the share of conspecific neighbors. With local
dispersal, small subplots contain fewer species, and with `dispersal` ≤ 1 the
species–area curve is steeper than with global dispersal. With local dispersal,
the probability that two cells contain the same species decreases with distance,
as expected.
Dispersal distances of 2 and 3 cells give almost the same richness as global
dispersal.

### Environmental filtering

::: {.expectation}
**Expectation.** Environmental filtering sorts species along the gradient, so
the correlation between trait and environment should increase with
`environment`. With local dispersal, offspring stay in the habitat of their
parents (species sorting); with global dispersal, many offspring land in
unsuitable cells (mass effects), which weakens the match between traits and
environment and reduces the differences between parts of the grid
[@mouquet2003]. The effect on richness can go either way: environmental
heterogeneity increases richness through niche partitioning in most empirical
studies [@stein2014], but in an area of fixed size, narrow niches reduce the
area available to each species and can reduce richness [@allouche2012]. With
the default niche width, a species finds good conditions only in a narrow band
of the gradient. Daughter species keep the traits of their founder, so closely
related species occupy similar positions on the gradient; such niche
conservatism together with environmental filtering is expected to make local
communities phylogenetically clustered [@webb2002] (not measured by the
indicators here). For tree shape, we found
no consistent prediction.
:::

```{r environment, echo = FALSE, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5, fig.cap = "Indicators against the strength of environmental filtering, for global and local dispersal."}
response(main, "environment", "environment", group = "dispersal")
```

**Result.** With local dispersal, already weak filtering (`environment = 0.25`)
makes the correlation between trait and environment almost perfect
(`r val("environment", "corTraitEnv", dispersal = "1", environment = 0.25)`),
whereas with global dispersal it stays at
`r val("environment", "corTraitEnv", dispersal = "global", environment = 1)` even
at `environment = 1`, as expected from mass effects. Richness increases with the
strength of filtering in both cases, so niche partitioning dominates over the
loss of area per species. Filtering makes the trees more balanced (Colless index
below 0) and increases the gamma statistic, i.e. branching is even more
concentrated towards the present than in the neutral model. A possible
explanation is that lineages adapted to different parts of the gradient persist
for a long time, while species within each part turn over as in the neutral
model; the speciation rate does not depend on richness, so no slowdown of
branching is expected [@phillimore2008]. With global dispersal, filtering lowers
the share of conspecific neighbors; with local dispersal, it changes it little.

### Strength of selection

::: {.expectation}
**Expectation.** With `fitnessBaseMortalityRatio = 1`, every death is random
and the model is neutral whatever the fitness; larger values make more deaths
depend on fitness. We therefore expect the effects of environmental filtering
and density dependence to increase with `fitnessBaseMortalityRatio`, starting
from the neutral values.
:::

```{r selection, echo = FALSE, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5, fig.cap = "Indicators against fitnessBaseMortalityRatio, with environmental filtering (environment = 1) or density dependence (density = 1)."}
response(main, "selection", "fitnessBaseMortalityRatio", group = "environment", log = "x")
```

**Result.** With `fitnessBaseMortalityRatio = 1`, both scenarios give the values
of the neutral model with local dispersal, as expected. With environmental
filtering, richness keeps increasing up to the largest value
(`r val("selection", "richness", environment = 1, fitnessBaseMortalityRatio = 50, digits = 3)`
species at 50). With density dependence, the spread of the competition trait
almost reaches its maximum already at 2, and richness increases only slightly.

### Density dependence

::: {.expectation}
**Expectation.** In the model, an individual is fitter the more its
competition trait differs from those of its neighbors. Because the traits
within a species are similar, this acts like conspecific negative density
dependence, as in the Janzen-Connell hypothesis. Such density dependence is
expected to increase species richness and to make abundances more even
[@chave2002; @levi2019]; its
effect depends on how far offspring disperse relative to the neighborhood
[@adler2005]. It should reduce the share of conspecific neighbors. Competition
on a trait favors dissimilar trait values, so the spread of the competition
trait should increase; species may form groups of similar trait values rather
than spreading evenly along the trait axis [@scheffer2006].
:::

```{r density, echo = FALSE, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5, fig.cap = "Indicators against the strength of density dependence, for two neighborhood radii (densityCut)."}
response(main, "density", "density", group = "densityCut")
```

**Result.** Density dependence reduces the share of conspecific neighbors, as
expected, but increases richness only slightly (from
`r val("density", "richness", density = 0, densityCut = 1, digits = 3)` to
`r val("density", "richness", density = 1, densityCut = 1, digits = 3)` species)
and Shannon diversity.
Already at `density = 0.25`, the standard deviation of the competition trait
rises to `r val("density", "sdCompetitionTrait", density = 0.25, densityCut = 1)`,
close to its maximum of 0.5 for traits in $[0, 1]$: the competition traits split
into two groups at the ends of the trait range. Stronger density dependence or a
larger neighborhood changes the indicators little in these runs; density
dependence was redesigned in
[#172](https://github.com/TheoreticalEcology/EcoPhyloSim/pull/172) (see the
vignette Model history).

### Environment and density dependence combined

::: {.expectation}
**Expectation.** Environmental filtering favors similar species in the same
place, and density dependence favors dissimilar neighbors, so the two
processes can mask each other in the patterns [@kraft2015]. Because the two
fitness terms were added in the version of these runs (before #172), the model
is neutral there if both are > 0 and `environment + density` ≤ 1.
:::

```{r envdensity, echo = FALSE, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5, fig.cap = "Indicators against environment, for three strengths of density dependence."}
response(main, "envDensity", "environment", group = "density")
```

**Result.** With `environment = density = 0.5`, the indicators have the values of
the neutral model, as expected. Combined with environmental filtering, density
dependence reduces richness (with `environment = 0.5`:
`r val("envDensity", "richness", environment = 0.5, density = 1, digits = 3)`
species with and
`r val("envDensity", "richness", environment = 0.5, density = 0, digits = 3)`
without `density = 1`), whereas on its own it increases richness slightly.

### Assembly processes and dispersal

The four combinations of environmental filtering (`environment` = 0 or 1) and
density dependence (`density` = 0 or 1), each with global and local
dispersal.

::: {.expectation}
**Expectation.** Environmental filtering should increase spatial aggregation
and the match between traits and environment, and density dependence should
reduce aggregation; both are expected to increase richness (see the sections
above). With both processes, their effects on the patterns can partly cancel
[@kraft2015], and dispersal can change how strongly each process shows
[@mouquet2003; @adler2005].
:::

```{r assembly, echo = FALSE, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5, fig.cap = "Indicators for the four combinations of environmental filtering and density dependence, for global and local dispersal."}
a <- main$settings$block == "assembly"
main$settings$scenario[a] <- c("neutral", "env.", "dens.", "both")[
  1 + main$settings$environment[a] + 2 * main$settings$density[a]]
response(main, "assembly", "scenario", group = "dispersal", xlab = "")
```

**Result.** Environmental filtering increases richness and the match between
traits and environment, much more with local than with global dispersal.
Contrary to the expectation, it does not increase spatial aggregation (see
Environmental filtering). Density dependence reduces aggregation with local
dispersal, and, combined with filtering, it reduces rather than increases
richness (see Environment and density dependence combined).

### Niche width

::: {.expectation}
**Expectation.** Narrower niches mean stronger filtering. Following the idea of
limiting similarity, more species with narrow niches can be packed along the
gradient, but narrow niches also reduce the area available to each species,
which increases the risk of extinction [@allouche2012]. Richness may therefore
peak at an intermediate niche width. The correlation between trait and
environment should be highest for narrow niches.
:::

```{r nichewidth, echo = FALSE, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5, fig.cap = "Indicators against the niche width (environment = 1), for global and local dispersal."}
response(main, "nicheWidth", "nicheWidth", group = "dispersal", log = "x")
```

**Result.** With global dispersal, richness is highest at intermediate niche
widths, as expected, but the correlation between trait and environment increases
with niche width (from
`r val("nicheWidth", "corTraitEnv", dispersal = "global", nicheWidth = 0.01)` to
`r val("nicheWidth", "corTraitEnv", dispersal = "global", nicheWidth = 0.3)`).
A possible reason is that with narrow niches and global dispersal, almost all
offspring land in unsuitable cells, so that fitness is low everywhere and
filtering is weak. With
local dispersal, traits match the environment closely at all widths, and richness
is highest for the narrowest niches.

### Density dependence measured from mortality

Field studies estimate conspecific negative density dependence (CNDD) from
the mortality of individuals in relation to the number of conspecific
neighbors [@comita2010; @hulsmann2024]. The same can be done with the model
output (`getMortalityData()`): for the last five generations of each run, a
logistic regression of death on the number of conspecifics within a radius of
2 cells, with a separate intercept per species, gives one CNDD coefficient per
run; positive values mean that mortality increases with the number of
conspecific neighbors.

::: {.expectation}
**Expectation.** In the neutral model, mortality does not depend on
neighbors, so the coefficient should be close to 0; this is a check of the analysis.
With density dependence, it should be positive. With environmental filtering
and local dispersal, conspecific neighbors indicate suitable habitat, so
mortality may decrease with their number, which would hide density dependence
in such an analysis. In tropical forests, rare species show stronger CNDD than
common ones [@comita2010; @hulsmann2024]. However, the number of conspecific
neighbors is only a proxy for the actual interactions, and in survival analyses
this biases the per-species estimates more for abundant than for rare species,
which can create a negative relationship between CNDD and abundance even if it
does not exist [@detto2019]. In the model, all species have the same density
dependence, so a relationship between the per-species slopes and abundance,
in particular in the neutral model, indicates such a bias.
:::

```{r cndd, echo = FALSE, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 3.5, fig.cap = "Left: CNDD coefficient per scenario and dispersal (replicate mean and 95% confidence interval; dashed: no effect). Right: CNDD slope of single species against their abundance with local dispersal, without (neutral) and with density dependence (all replicates; lines: linear fits)."}
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
f <- merge(main$settings[a, ], main$cndd[main$cndd$block == "assembly", ])
f$ci <- qt(0.975, pmax(f$n - 1, 1)) * f$sd / sqrt(f$n)
f <- f[order(f$density, f$environment, f$dispersal), ]
sc <- unique(f$scenario)
xpos <- match(f$scenario, sc) + ifelse(f$dispersal == "global", -0.1, 0.1)
plot(xpos, f$mean, pch = 16, col = cols[1 + (f$dispersal != "global")], xaxt = "n",
     xlab = "", ylab = "CNDD coefficient", ylim = range(c(0, f$mean - f$ci, f$mean + f$ci)))
axis(1, at = seq_along(sc), labels = sc)
ciBars(xpos, f$mean, f$ci, cols[1 + (f$dispersal != "global")])
abline(h = 0, lty = 2)
legend("topleft", legend = c("global", "1"), pch = 16, col = cols[1:2], title = "dispersal", bty = "n")
sp <- lapply(c(neutral = 0, density = 1), function(dens)
  main$cnddSpecies[main$cnddSpecies$block == "assembly" &
                     main$cnddSpecies$setting == settingId(main, "assembly", environment = 0,
                                                           density = dens, dispersal = "1"), ])
all <- do.call(rbind, sp)
plot(all$abundance, all$slope, log = "x", type = "n", xlab = "Abundance", ylab = "CNDD slope")
for (k in seq_along(sp)) {
  points(sp[[k]]$abundance, sp[[k]]$slope, pch = 16, col = adjustcolor(cols[k + 2], 0.4))
  abline(lm(slope ~ log10(abundance), sp[[k]]), col = cols[k + 2], lwd = 2)
}
abline(h = 0, lty = 2)
legend("topright", legend = names(sp), pch = 16, col = cols[3:4], bty = "n")
par(op)
```

**Result.** As expected, the CNDD coefficient is close to 0 in the neutral model
and positive with density dependence. Environmental filtering makes it negative,
and with both processes it is negative as well, so filtering hides the density
dependence in this analysis. Contrary to the expectation, the effect is stronger with global
than with local dispersal. The per-species slopes depend only weakly on abundance
in the scenarios shown. In the neutral model with global dispersal, a linear fit
of the slopes against log abundance is negative in all settings of the
speciation rate and grid size (not shown), although no species has density
dependence; this agrees with the bias described by @detto2019, but the trend is
weak compared with the scatter of the slopes.

# Fitting the model to data

EcoPhyloSim has no tractable likelihood: the probability of observed data, such
as a species map, abundances and a phylogeny, cannot be calculated for given
parameters. Its parameters can still be estimated by simulation-based
inference [@hartig2011; @cranmer2020]: the model is run for many parameter
values drawn from a prior, and the simulations that resemble the data are kept,
or used to train an estimator. Data and simulations are usually compared through
summary statistics, such as those of `calculateSummaryStatistics()`. Which
statistics are used, and how the data are observed (e.g. as subplots, see
`localPlots()`), decides what can be learned; the patterns in the chapter
Emerging patterns show which outputs respond to which parameters, and how long
runs must be to reach equilibrium.

## Approximate Bayesian computation

The package contains a pipeline for rejection ABC. `runPhylosimAnalysis()`
draws parameters from priors (functions that return one value each), runs the
simulations in parallel and saves the parameters and summary statistics in
chunks, which `chunkwiseCleanup()`, `combineChunks()` and
`prepareForAnalysis()` combine into tables of parameters and scaled summaries. `rejectionSamplePhylosimAnalysis()` then tests how well
the parameters can be recovered: it takes some of the simulations as
pseudo-observed data, estimates their parameters from the closest of the other
simulations and returns the true and the estimated values. With many
summaries, it can first reduce them to predictions of the parameters
(`which = "saABC"`: semi-automatic ABC with the package abctools; `which = "rf"`:
a random forest with the package ranger).

```{r abc, eval = FALSE}
priors <- list(specRate = function() runif(1, 0.5, 8),
               negativeDD = function() runif(1, 0, 1),
               environment = function() runif(1, 0, 1))
# runs long enough to reach equilibrium (see Time to equilibrium)
fixed <- list(x = 50, y = 50, dispersal = 1, runs = 50000, calculateSummaries = TRUE)
runPhylosimAnalysis(priors, fixed, nRuns = 10000, outDir = "abc", summariesOnly = TRUE)
chunkwiseCleanup("abc")
combineChunks("abc/cleaned_up", "summary_clean")
combineChunks("abc/cleaned_up", "param_clean")
prepareForAnalysis("abc", priors)
recovery <- rejectionSamplePhylosimAnalysis("abc/analysis_ready/parameters",
                                            "abc/analysis_ready/summaries_scaled",
                                            nDraws = 100, which = c("none", "rf"))
```

Such runs need thousands of simulations, each run to equilibrium, so they
take long (see the section Runtime). For observed data, the same table of
simulated parameters and summaries can be used with general ABC packages, e.g.
abc [@csillery2012], or abcrf, which estimates the parameters with random
forests, is robust to the choice of summary statistics and needs no tolerance
level [@raynal2019]. The observed summaries must be computed in the same way as
the simulated ones and scaled with the standard deviations of the simulated
summaries.

## Neural simulation-based inference

Neural methods train a neural network on the simulations, to approximate the
posterior directly (neural posterior estimation) or the likelihood (neural
likelihood estimation) [@cranmer2020]. They can learn informative summaries
from high-dimensional outputs, and a network trained once can be applied to new
data sets without new simulations (amortized inference). Python libraries such
as sbi [@tejero2020] and BayesFlow [@radev2023] implement these methods; the
simulations can be produced with `runPhylosimAnalysis()` and exported from R,
e.g. as tables of parameters and summaries.
